utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The telephone doesn't work again. So for a few weeks it worked normally, except for that one day when I drew your attention to that, and since the beginning of this week, it hasn't been working, any number I dial. I dial the same numbers that I've been dialling over these past few days and weeks. The machine says that this line is not authorised, not even for telephone calls within The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've made some inquiries. We understand the position to be that you can telephone your associates in Belgrade, but we'll make some further inquiries into that because we need to understand the position fully. Yes. We'll continue with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely who I've been calling, my associates in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, can you please give to the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: May the 24th, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In the village of Bellanice at Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So in which municipality is Belanica located?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What's your profession?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I'm a journalist by profession. I worked for the Rilindja newspaper, teacher at the primary school Thismaich [phoen] Mali, and an activist for reconciliation of feuds.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zogaj, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 25th and 26th of April, 1999, and you gave a statement while you were in Tirana. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you were subsequently interviewed on the 12th and the 18th of June, 2002 [sic], and you gave a second statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In June 2001, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And on the 3rd of February this year, you attend a meeting with members of the Office of the Prosecutor and an appointed officer of the Tribunal, and at that meeting, you were provided with a copy of your statement in the Albanian language. You had an opportunity to review and to confirm that its contents are true?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it, made some corrections regarding the translation made by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At that meeting, you made an addendum to correct the translations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I would like at that moment to just introduce the statement formally into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be Exhibit 108.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is a journalist working for a newspaper and he has reported several materials during the conflict in 1998. He describes the situation in Suva Reka from 20 March 1999, when the OSCE KVM mission pulled out from Kosovo. The streets were empty of civilian Albanians, but there was a heavy presence of Serb police and military. On the same day, the Serbs attacked villages in the area and people started to flee to safer places, like Belanica, in his home village, Belanica. He describes the situation in Suva Reka on the 25th of March, 1999, including the killings and burning of houses. The witness mentioned victims and survivors from the massacre in Suva Reka by name. All the villages in the areas of Suva Reka and Malisevo were attacked from March 1999 onwards. The inhabitants fled and gathered in a big field in the centre of Belanica, so that by March 31st, there were about 80.000 people there. The witness also describes that on April 1st, Belanica was shelled, and police, military, and paramilitary forces, numbering about 1.500, subsequently entered the village. The Serb forces forced people from their houses, looted their homes, loaded the goods on the trucks, and set the houses on fire. Many young men and women were taken to the school and detained. No one has seen them since. The witness describes that around 150 civilian Albanians were killed that day. And they were then forced, the witness and his family, to leave Belanica in a convoy. The convoy was directed into two directions. One part of the convoy was headed via Blace-Suva Reka- Albanian border, the other one via Malisevo-Orahovac-Albanian border. During the trip, the convoy was stopped at a number of Serb checkpoints, where the Kosovar Albanians were beaten, robbed, and insulted. Members of the convoy, following the northern route via Malisevo, disappeared and have not been seen since. After 30 hours, the witness describes that he arrived at the Albanian border, where documents and vehicle number plates were seized. That's the summary of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you graduate from the Pristina university?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I graduated on December 1st, 1998 at the Prishtina university.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked as a journalist from 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I have been working, and I shall be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you graduated from the University of Pristina, could you briefly say how many Albanians studied together with you at the University of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I'm not competent to give a figure as to how many people studied there. I can only speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Together with you, there were -- or, rather, how many were there in your group?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I think I gave an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "group," Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean "group," the usual group of students studying at the university. Those who attend lectures together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand what that question means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not talking about a group here but a number of over 20.000 students who, as of 1990, or from 1990 to the end of the war, they followed study in private premises in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting anywhere. We're not getting anywhere. If you want to ask a precise question, Mr. Milosevic, do, but at the moment, we're not getting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite obvious, because this student doesn't even know how many people he studied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your written statement, in paragraph 3, inter alia, that as you were walking down the main road that passes through Rastane, Studencane and continues to Orahovac, you saw a convoy of army and police consisting of 14 tanks and armoured vehicles and that at that moment you realised that something terrible would happen. You say that in Rastane there was a police checkpoint. And the next sentence is: "The other areas were controlled by the KLA."

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I have not said that these areas were controlled by the KLA, and I think you have -- I think the sentence from the beginning is not quite correct. I think you do not understand what the sentence in itself means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does the sentence mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the OSCE mission leaving Kosova on March the 20th, when the signal was given for the mission to leave. And immediately after the departure of the OSCE mission, Serbian police, military, paramilitary, and civilian Serb forces assaulted the village of Rreshtan where, after 12.00, shelling -- continued shelling started against Studencan, Peqan e Vogel, Doberdolan, and others. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just answer my questions, because the other side, and you together with them, have opted for you not to testify but only to give a written statement. You are just supposed to answer my questions. And the sentence that you say that I've misquoted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not a matter for the witness how he testifies. It's a matter for the Court. So it's not fair to put that to him. But, Mr. Zogaj, you can help us with this: What is being -- what is being put to you is this sentence as it was read out. This is in the English, which I'm reading from. You've described what happened in the town when the observers withdrew. You left Suva Reka and were walking along the main road and you saw this convoy of Serb army and police which has been mentioned. You say: "I knew then that something terrible would happen." It says: "There was a Serb police checkpoint at Rreshtan." And then it goes on: "The other areas were controlled by the KLA." Now, that's the sentence you're being asked about, and perhaps you can tell us what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Naturally, the KLA occupied its own positions, and it was formed to protect the people of Kosova, whereas Serbian forces which the accused is -- and I hope the Tribunal find him guilty on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Please don't comment. Just give us your evidence. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately after the departure of the OSCE mission, and I saw them -- when I left, myself I saw the Suhareke city emptied of Albanians. Albanians were afraid of venturing into the streets where only Serbian police with civilian -- on civilian vehicles with no registration plates were. Some shops were open but there was nobody buying there. Nobody ventured out to go and buy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, we can read this. We have your statement. Time is limited. You are being asked about the areas controlled by the KLA. Now, is it right, as you say in your statement, that the other areas were controlled by them? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The regions as I have mentioned there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is unclear in that sentence then? From the beginning to the very end, it says: "Other areas were controlled by the KLA." Full stop. Your explanation was that I did not understand what it said there. What is unclear in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand this question at all. I don't know what you mean by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, I quoted that sentence to you. It's very short, only seven words, and it says: "The other areas were controlled by the KLA." In response to that, you said that I did not understand the sentence, and that that is not what you meant. What is controversial in this sentence? What is there that cannot be understood? It simply says: "The other areas were controlled by the KLA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has agreed that that is what he said. He Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can't add anything. There's no point arguing with him about it. That's what he said. Now, ask him something else about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked because once he said that I did not understand the sentence, and the second time he said that they were controlled by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say, since it is clear that these other areas that you speak of were controlled by the KLA, that attacks began; that is to say, a conflict between the army and the KLA. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Conflicts were always caused by the Serbian army, police, and paramilitary. And I've nothing to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I assume that that is your assertion, but it is obvious that the conflict was between the Serb forces, as you call them, and the KLA. And then you move on to the next sentence, which says, and I am quoting it quite precisely: "The population began to move out en masse towards quieter places." That is to say, refugees were leaving the area en masse, the area where fighting was taking place between the state forces and the terrorist organisation of the KLA. Is that the picture that you've been explaining?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: These were not state forces, and these others were not terrorist forces but defence forces, and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You left out, Mr. Milosevic, the sentence before. The sentence before was: "About 12.20 p.m., the first attacks began on the villages of Peqan, Studencan, and Doberdolan. The population began to move out en masse towards quieter places." Who was responsible for the attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paramilitary forces, Serbian police and military forces too, were responsible for the attacks. And the people left the areas, were scared of a possible massacre, as it happened in other places, as you know. And I have with me photographs of the Serbian police and army, showing what they did in Kosova. I've got it here with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment so we can follow the position. There were these attacks. Was there any defence or did the people just leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence was conducted by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what's being put to you is that the people fled because there was a conflict. Do you understand? That's the suggestion. Now, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The people were afraid because there was fighting going on, and therefore they left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've clarified that. Now we can even skip some questions in order to save time. It is obvious; refugees are leaving the area of conflict, like anywhere else. You say, towards the end of the first page: "A large number of people went to Bellanice and Banje because there had been no shooting or shelling at Bellanice. The heavy artillery reached into the KLA-controlled area, and they also used military aircraft, not only against KLA positions, but also against the civilian population." Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. First of all, the Serbian fighters - that is, the aircraft - observed the people, and then the next day there was shelling, and in the evening, only a few metres above the ground. I saw -- I have these notes. I have the time when they conducted these operations. Unfortunately, more than a thousand documents were burned, and if they had not been burned, I would be able to show you the photographs, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Yes. What do you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something: that some of the Serbian shelling on the village of Bllace, on the 28th of March, in the early hours of the morning, a Serbian military aircraft fired in the direction of the village but, fortunately, there were no casualties. In these documents, I have the notes about this shell that was fired on Bllace, and I can show you everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which villages did you see shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Bllace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask you something? Am I carrying out this cross-examination or is it you, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's quite unnecessary. If you don't ask questions which are clear, or if there are matters which the Chamber wants clarified, they will ask questions. Now, if you want to ask questions, do so now, or otherwise we'll bring this to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was this question that I put unclearly? Can you please tell me that so that I would be clearer from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your questions are much too long. They often contain assertions or speeches or comment. Those will be stopped and clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the death of four persons: Ramadan Sukaj, Hafiz Shala, Osman Elshani, and Albert, last name unknown.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Another name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you move on to say -- I'm reading what it says here in respect of these four persons, these four men. And then you say that you learned of this event. So my question is: You did not see this. You learnt of this. You heard about it.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please. As a journalist, I had the right to meet and to ask questions of people who had been evicted, who had survived death, including Sejdi Bytyci, the history teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your right to talk. I asked you a specific question, a concrete question. You didn't see it; you heard about it. Is that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: As a journalist, I have the right to ask people questions, and these things are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's another topic altogether. Of course journalists can talk to people. That's not what I'm asking you. All I'm asking you is about what you yourself said. You said you learnt of this event, and I'm asking you about you just learnt of it or whether you saw it as well.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself, but I have asked this person who had survived this massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mention attacks by Serb forces on the other side, and you also mention the village of Dragobil. As you're a journalist, I'm sure you knew everything that went on --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't mention Dragobil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the middle here of that page, which is page 4, it says -- and it's that small paragraph exactly in the middle of the page: "In Malisheva, a large convoy of Serbian police, military and paramilitaries had reached Malisheva from the direction of Orllat, consisting of 40 heavy military vehicles." I apologise to the interpreters for going fast. "I saw this from the hill at Banje. I saw these forces bombarding the villages of Banje, Dragobil, Gur I Bardh, and the surrounding areas." "I saw that from the hill in Banje." That's what it says. "I saw these forces bombarding the villages of Banje, Dragobil, Gur I Bardh," as it states in the original, "and the surrounding areas." So that's what I'm referring to: your mention of Dragobil and the surrounding areas around Dragobil. So you did mention Dragobil. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is true. It's true. And it's on this very same day five members of the Begaj family died, were casualties, one of whom these casualties was fatal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you the following: As you're a journalist, and you yourself say you know the circumstances that prevailed about the situation, do you know that in Dragobil the KLA had its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: At what time period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the time period while the Verification Mission was present too, of the OSCE, that time too, and during the time of KDOM and later on, from the beginning of the war onwards. So it is the period before the war and at the very beginning of the war as well.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I can't talk about the period before the war, but I can say anything you like about the period during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked if you know that Dragobil was the KLA headquarters. That's what's suggested. Can you assist us as to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer. It was -- it was the KLA's, but Serbian forces entered later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that four contacts, with representatives of the KLA in the village, in that village of Dragobil, there was a forward representative of the Kosovo Verification Mission and KDOM? Did you know about that? That was before the war too.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 7 in my version of your statement, in the middle of that page, before you go on to enumerate the names, you say the following -- it is the middle paragraph: "From 1.00 to 7.00 p.m., we were in the convoy, slowly advancing. The police had guided the population in two directions. One was in the direction of Malisheva and Rahovec and the other stream of people which we joined was in the direction of Bllace and Suhareke." I am quoting that paragraph so you know what my next question is going to be about and what it refers to. And it refers to the following sentence, which says: "At this moment, we learned of other people in the village of Bellanice who had been murdered by the police, including the following persons," and then you go on to enumerate. And you say again that you did not see it but heard it. You learnt it from other people. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to -- allow me to say something about -- allow me to say something about what I experienced myself, because we're bypassing this. Allow me to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that you have a lot to say to us, but please bear in mind that we have your statement and we have read it. Please stick to the question. We will get on better with simple answers. The question is whether you saw those killings or that's what you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first murder that I saw was the murder of Agim Bytyci from the village of Nishor, who was mentally handicapped. The policeman killed them, and you are the man who gave them the orders for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do not comment, Mr. Zogaj. You are here to give evidence. Tell us what you saw and heard. Now, you are being asked about the village of Belanica, and it was put to you that this was something you learned. In your statement, you list the people who were killed there. What you can tell us is how you heard what the circumstances were of your hearing of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the expulsions, the police, army, and paramilitaries, while entering the village, killed immediately the 73-year-old Izet Hoxha. I met his wife, Bahtishahe, who told me this. And then close to a shop called Vatra, there were four bodies lying, which were not identified. During the journey to Temeqin, there was a 40-year-old man mutilated, and I saw this body with my own eyes. It was a male body. And while I was in the village, I also heard of the deaths from shelling of Nazlije Kryeziu and her daughter, 11 years old, Drita Kryeziu, who were refugees from the village of Reti in Rahovec municipality. These are some of the murders that I know of, and there were many, many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the essence of my question was as follows, and I expected a yes or no answer: What you describe here was not something that you saw but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something that you heard about, learnt from others. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's said that. There's no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 9, at the end of the first, what we heard at the beginning in the summary of your testimony it says, and I'm quoting: "At Kukes, in the following days, I heard from other people who had travelled from Bellanice that on the 1st and 2nd of April, 1999, as a result of the Serbian police action during those days, that up to 150 people were killed." So that's the whole sentence, from one full stop to another. "I heard from other people." So once again, what you're testifying is not something that you saw yourself but something that you heard from other people. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you have another statement which was mentioned at the beginning, and I'm just going to refer to that statement very briefly because it's just a little different, slightly different from the previous one. And in paragraph 3, at the beginning of that other statement, you say: "According to my assessment, in Bellanice, on the 1st of April, there were about 80.000 people." Now, in your first statement, you wrote that in Belanica you saw thousands of people. Now -- you said thousands of people to begin with. Now, that figure in your second statement, testifying about the same event, you have increased to 80.000 people. Do you have an explanation for that? Why is there such a big difference between your first statement and your second statement pertaining to one and the same event?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I will tell everything. From the beginning of May 1998, the first wave of refugees reached Bellanice from Drenica, from Rahovec, whilst on March the 20th, 1999, and I've got dates, hours, the time when they arrived, which place they came from, what they said, and on the 29th, 30th, and 31st of March, the number reached 80.000. And I've got documents and everything here. I've got them with me. I've got everything here. Everything else was burned. I also have a photograph dated 28 and 29 March which shows the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. I just asked you why there was such a lot of difference between your first and second statements about the same event. Because in one you say thousands and in the other you say 80.000. So can you give an explanation about that or not? But if what you have just said is your explanation, then let it stand. Let that be your explanation. It is sufficiently clear. Now, at the end of that first page of your second statement, you are talking about different events. And I'm not going to go into them now because they're not the subject of my next question for you, but I'm just going to quote the sentence I do wish to ask you about. You say: "I saw that with my own eyes as an international journalist and not as a KLA journalist." Now my question is as follows: Were you a KLA journalist, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No, I was not a KLA journalist. I was a journalist with the Rilindja newspaper, and I've got all the notes pertaining to the Rilindja newspaper here. And this -- the writing on the 5th of May, 1998, shows this, shows best how Serbian police established a presence in the village of Dulje and what they did to the civilian population. It is half a page long and contains three photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was just whether you were also a KLA journalist, because you wrote here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's denied it. He's denied it. You've heard what he said. Were you -- just so we can understand this, were you working full time for the newspaper Rilindja or was it part time, sending in the odd article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the year 1996, and I possess documentation on this, I've always been working for Rilindja. If you wish, I can show them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, why did you add the phrase "not as a KLA journalist"? What did you mean by this phrase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've put it there simply to show that we've been unable to go into areas controlled by the Serbian police and the army but only in those areas that were controlled by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a very good answer. Now, you mentioned Rilindja. When did you actually work for Rilindja? In what period? From what date to what date? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that exactly. From June the 20th, 1996 to the present, to this very day. And I will probably die before I leave Rilindja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is -- was Rilindja published regularly throughout the time that you worked for it? Did it come out on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Not on Sundays. There were occasions when you yourself stopped its publication. You were the one who stopped the publication of Rilindja many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether Rilindja was published regularly throughout the time. How many times did it not come out for any reason?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I cannot say how many times, because it's people in the administration who should know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're a journalist working regularly. Now, do you say that Rilindja was banned on several occasions? Is that what you're saying, that some of the issues were banned?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You banned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Are you claiming that certain issues of the Rilindja were banned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's said they were, and he's added that you banned it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I claim that nobody banned the publishing of newspapers in Kosovo. Now, my next question: Could you buy various newspapers in the Albanian language almost at every corner? In Pristina, at least.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Only on -- on the corner inhabited by Serbs there was no possibility of buying it; otherwise, yes. At that time, Rilindja, when I first started work for it, was called Bujku, because in 1990, not only Rilindja but all other Albanian media were closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could you work in a closed Rilindja from 1996 up until the war if Rilindja had been closed down? How were you able to work for it then?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Rilindja continued being published -- Rilindja continued being published after some specific permission was granted. Otherwise -- at the whims of yourself, your police and your Serbian forces could close it down. The newspaper was under censure. And after that, only after that, it was allowed to get through to the readers. Serbian police beat me several times simply as a result of the fact of me having been a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am hearing for the first time that censorship was introduced. Now, how did this function? How did this work work? What kind of censorship? Who was in charge of enforcing the censorship?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I do not understand how you could possibly say that it is the first time you hear of any censure when every single order came from yourself, beginning with the primary schools and up to the university, from the poisoning, massive poisoning of over 7.232 pupils. They were not allowed to write about it, about the truth, but we found a way of doing it in order to defy the enemy. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're not testifying about the uni-national poisoning in Kosovo now, but about other events. And a moment ago you said that Rilindja came out every day except Sundays. Does that mean that your paper was censored every day when it went to print? Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm indebted to give him an answer to this, because I was one of those who was poisoned on 23rd of March, 1990, and to this day I continue to suffer aftereffects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us about the censorship of the paper. Can you give us some idea of how often it happened, how many issues were banned or how often they were banned? Can you give us a rough idea of what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give exact figures, because it was banned on several occasions. And at the end, following the NATO air bombardment against Serb or Slav targets, all newspapers were banned and hundreds of people were beaten and persecuted by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: During all the years that you worked for Rilindja - even very roughly - for all those years, how many issues of the Rilindja do you claim were banned, during all the years that you worked for the newspaper? Give us a very rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I'm not competent to give this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as a journalist, do you know that in view of the Yugoslav laws and the laws of the Republic of Serbia, censorship, that you're referring to here, is illegal and impossible?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It was fully feasible by yourself. The newspaper was not published on time, and several issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It occurred with several issues over a number of years. Now, I claim that they were not even several issues, but I don't think we'll be able to establish that today. So let's go back to your own statement. On page 3 of your second statement, you go back once again to the subject that is actually the substance of your statement, because you say: "On the 30th of March, I personally saw 44 armoured vehicles belonging to the Serb police and army which had arrived from Caralluka as reinforcements to the already-existing units in --"

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you let me read the whole of the quotation out first, please. Now, from there, as well as from their positions in Caralluka, in the Malisevo municipality, they fired in the direction of Terpeza, Ladrovac, Senik and Banja, also Dragobil. The units attacked these moving targets. Now, you are talking about reinforcements, the reinforcements coming to be reinforcements to the police and army forces in the Dragobil area, which was where the KLA had its headquarters, and the conflicts going on there. Now, from what you're saying, you're clearly defining conflicts between the forces of the defence of the country, on the one hand, and the terrorist KLA organisation on the other. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you ask questions in that form, you know you will get an answer denying that these are organisations as you describe them. There's no point with witnesses trying to make your points. It's a waste of time. If you want to ask if there was a conflict, do, but no point making speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the American representative for the Balkans, Robert Gelbard, defined the KLA as being a terrorist organisation in February 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the witness how he defined it. Now, help us with this: Was there a conflict at the time that you're talking about, when, you say, the Serb police and army were seen by you coming to reinforce troops in Malisevo and firing, as you describe it, as they were moving along? That's what you describe in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is true. They did not fire in the direction of the KLA fighters, but against civilian targets, where there were killings from the shelling. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If that is true, that what you've said, how come it says at the end of the page: "The KLA --" I'm quoting. I'm quoting every word. "The KLA had positions in villages such as Bllace, Gallusha, which covered three villages: Peqan, Sllapuzhan, Semetishte. In addition to that, Doberdolan, and in the mountains, in the municipality of Suva Reka, Milanovic, Dragobil, again Dragobil, and Gajrak, in the municipality of Malisheva." So you have been talking about here positions of the KLA, where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you say that it was the army that was firing at civilians. You said this. And again you refer to Dragobil in this set of villages where you speak of the entire area in which there were KLA units. And then the paragraph says: "The KLA had its positions," et cetera, et cetera. Doesn't this deny what you've been saying all along, your very own statement?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues...] had to do with kilometres. I will answer about Malisheva here. And I said before, and I'll say it again: The KLA positions were not attacked. The civilian population was attacked from a distance. And as for the other parts of Suhareke municipality I mentioned - and I didn't mention the names of the villages because they're not available to me - it is true that the KLA was staying there and that it fought to protect the civilian population for about ten days. But it was impossible to defend what is called the Pagarushe area, around Dragobil and Caravrana, and Serbian police and paramilitaries went in and plundered and burned everything that was Albanian there. And in the end, the entire population took shelter in Bellanice. That is the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that you are now asserting, in terms of what you said just now, that the KLA was fighting to protect civilians. That's what you said. And a little while ago, you said that the army and the police did not attack the KLA. Does that mean, on the basis of your statement, that the KLA was shooting at the army and the police that was not attacking the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Do you think that they should all be killed and people should just stand by and have all the Albanians killed? That was why the KLA defended the civilian population. There was no army that kills the population, apart from the Serbian army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't attack the KLA. That is your assertion. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The population was attacked with tanks and with cannon, and then the KLA entered this melee too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You have given a sufficient explanation in terms of this particular logic of warfare. Let's go back to your professional work, because you say that you looked at things as an international journalist. What is this international newspaper that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It's not an international newspaper. I said that -- I mentioned I'm a member of the International Association of Journalists, based in Brussels, and here is the press card that I have. It's not a newspaper; it's an identity card. Here it is, international press card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't work for any international newspapers, not a single one. I mean, independently of your membership card, I'm asking you whether you worked for an international newspaper.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't work for an international newspaper. I'm a member of the International Association of Journalists. I worked for Rilindja, and I think that the Federation of the International Association of Journalists takes care of journalists' rights, and Rilindja is a member of this association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning that at all. I just asked you whether you worked for an international newspaper, and I got an answer, and there is no need to go into any further explanations. You wrote that you were on a commission of the Crisis Staff. In which capacity were you on this commission? As a member of the KLA or not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: He always mentions the KLA, and you never mention your own forces. I can't give an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't argue. Take no notice of the comment. You were asked about the commission, and at what capacity were you on the commission? Were you on it in any particular capacity or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of capacity? What commission here? As a journalist, I have my duty to my homeland, to go to crisis areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it that there's a reference in your statement to an anticipated flow of people coming into Belanica, and you say: "We created a commission of the emergency council for Belanica, which was supposed to find shelter for the incoming people." There may be some other references intended, but as far as that's concerned, were you on it in any particular capacity or were you just trying to help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only trying to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote here that you gave instructions to the locals. On the basis of what did you give instructions to the locals?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't recollect writing this, but I can say that in the village there was a commission formed for accommodation of these people who arrived, and I kept track of events as they happened, and I wrote about them in the newspaper, and here are my articles for Rilindja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that on that commission, you were in the capacity of some kind of a volunteer, if I understand you correctly. They admitted you as a voluntary member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Everybody helped each other, and if the commission hadn't been formed to help the needy --- as we say in Kosova, this commission was very necessary. When somebody is in need, then this need has to be met, if it is possible. If it's not possible, then, in the case of these people who had been expelled, people were left outside in the rain and the snow, without food. And this happened. People were outside in the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you write about the traffic police having helped you. That is towards the end, on page 7. "Fifteen minutes later, the vehicles of the traffic police escorted us to the centre of Prizren," et cetera, et cetera. It seems that the traffic police helped you more than that commission of yours. Is that right or is that not right? Because you say that you gave instructions that they should enter vehicles, that they should get out of vehicles, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Where was this traffic police? In which place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here, in your statement. They escorted you to Prizren. They helped you go to Prizren. That is what you wrote in your own statement.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: As I wrote, and I will say clearly: After the police expelled us from Bellanice, by force - beating people, killing people - on the road, at the village of Lubishte, in the evening, we were stopped by the traffic police, and they told us -- asked us where we were from - and we were the first vehicle in the convoy - and we said that we had come from Bellanice. And the police and the paramilitaries and others, in the yard of the police station of Lubishte, were singing Chetnik songs. The traffic police told us, "In that you come from Bellanice, and there are a lot of you, you must wait a little here, and from here we will escort you as far as the road to Zhur to go to Albania." I have told the Tribunal before that I'm grateful to these policemen because the others didn't give any kind of help, but you can't say that these police helped more than the village commission did. You absolutely can't say that. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You are here in the position to say what is true and what is not true. Since you're a journalist and since you followed events closely, are you familiar with the following: On the 29th of March, 1999, when on the local road between your municipality, that is to say Suva Reka and Orahovac, in the village of Rreshtan, in the territory of your municipality, that is to say Suva Reka, Albanian terrorists shot at members of the police who were in a GAZ official vehicle? This was on the 20th of March, 1999; that is to say, before the war started. Are you familiar with this event, with the fact that it took place?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The war was already happening. And what you say, indeed there could have been people killed by Serbian forces. And you have denied this. You have never told the media that people were killed in Rreshtan and other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're getting some way from the matter. Mr. Milosevic, you've had past the hour now. If you have another question, you can ask it, or otherwise that's the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have many more questions, but I think that part of this time what you restricted to one hour was used by you, too, and also in part by the witness with his unnecessary explanations. I think that you could extend this time to me, this time that you had economised with to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had more than the hour to allow for that. Now, do you want to ask him one more question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do. How would I not want to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about this although you're a journalist. And are you aware of anything in the territory of your municipality of Suva Reka of any crimes committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Over Serbs, over Albanians, and the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Why don't you mention the murders that you committed yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not an answer. Now, the question you were asked was: Are you aware of any crimes committed by the KLA in the municipality of Suva Reka? Now, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of any cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to try to explain a few facts which I believe remained unclear, of course bearing in mind the written statement only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, when you gave this statement of yours, as far as I can see according to these minutes, you started on the 20th of March, 1999. Is that right, the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And a little while ago when you talked about all of this, first you came to 11.30 and then you answered what you answered a little while ago to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, and then you said at twenty past twelve the first attacks began against the villages, and then you mentioned the villages. So it was on the 20th, not the 25th of May that these attacks occurred against these villages. That's what you said here, and very precisely at that, at twenty past twelve.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: That's not true. You haven't understood. On the 20th of March, at 12.30, whereas on the 25th, that is when the massacre at Suhareke took place when hundreds of people were killed. And from 1998 to 1999, 522 people were killed in Suhareke. You've mixed this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, believe me, that is not what I asked you. I just have your own statement in front of me. On the 20th of March, and now you say quite precisely on the 20th of March what happened at 11.30 and then what happen at 12.20, and that the first attacks started. That is what you already explained in response to -- is it the way it's been written here or is it not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was on this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it's on the 20th, not the 25th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 20th of March. I said at the beginning, I will say it again; this happened on the 20th of March. Don't get me confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not getting -- it's not my intention at all to get you confused. Now, in the first paragraph of your statement, you mentioned a great many villages. You mentioned that on that day, the Serb forces attacked several dozens of villages, and you mentioned a great many of these villages. Are all of these villages villages that were under the KLA control and protection?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: These villages were attacked. Of course the KLA was there. But in the end, all these villages were burned by the barbarians, by criminals. That is the truth. And I have photographs of the burned houses and the destroyed mosques which were destroyed by the Serbian army and police. This cannot be avoided. This is the truth. This was seen by the OSCE mission, and it was also seen immediately after the war, on the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would just kindly ask you to deal with the things that are here in your statement. I would just like to complete this subject by the following: You also said, in relation to the 20th of March, and only then do you move on to the 25th of March, you say that there were artillery attacks that the KLA held by the Serb forces and then aircraft were used, and that was also on the 20th of March, according to your statement.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say on the 20th of March. Please look at it properly. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said during the time of the OSCE mission. It's all written here. I've also written the number of this missile which was 1.5 metres with the year of when it was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it was before the 25th. All of this was before the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No. This -- this happened on the 28th. On the 28th this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's how I'd like to finish. Today is the first time you mentioned the 28th of March. The 28th of March and the aeroplane were first mentioned by you today. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It's not the first time. I mentioned it before. I mentioned it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to insist. You have his previous statement, and this would conclude the first part of what I wanted to deal with. Now the second statement, just one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second statement that was given on the 12th and 18th of June, 2001. The first, second, third, fourth -- fifth paragraph of the English version. You said here that in 1998, in 1998 - that's what it says in your statement - there were refugees in your village from the area of Drenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. From the village Llapushnik, from Vukovfc, Orllat, and others. I can mention all by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many refugees were there then in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: One to ten hundred. They're all refugees. All are refugees. So regardless of the numbers, one, two, all are refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many people left Drenica then? I agree. In 1998, Drenica was under whose control? Was all of Drenica under KLA control then?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No, because Drenica is not 100 or 200 metres. It's a wide area, and the KLA could in no way control the entire territory given the presentation of Serbian forces for years on end; not on that particular day but for years on end. Kumarani was also under the Serbian police and army. People were always beaten up and there was a lot of plundering. And one of those people -- I was one of those people. I was taken by the police in 1994 and possessions were taken off me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in 1998. There were refugees who came to your village. At that time, due to the conflicts that were taking place between the KLA and the Yugoslav army or police, were people moving to more peaceful areas? Yes or no. And let us conclude with that.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No one in Kumarani was. There were only Serbian tanks, police, army, and the paramilitary. The population had to go somewhere for safe shelter, and that's why they sought quieter spots. And if you want to confirm whether the people left or not, let me tell you what happened earlier, not on that particular day alone, because I went through that. And if you're not interested, I'm not interested either. Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am certainly interested in that, but here we are dealing with your statement only. We cannot deal with things that are not contained in your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In your second statement, you said that because of the shelling of the above-mentioned villages, and you mentioned several villages, from 20 March on, the villagers start to flee to Belanica. I want to clarify, Mr. Zogaj, one matter. The villagers, they fled because of the attack, because of the shelling and the actions of the Serbian forces that you described, or the villagers left because of the subsequent fighting between the -- that happened between the Serb forces and the KLA that was defending the village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You said on March the 20th. The civilian population did not leave on March the 20th. But from March the 20th, people reached Bellanice because it was a quieter place. And the whole area was in flames. Basa Hoxhaj was in flames. There was killing. There was pillaging. Serbian police and army went into the villages with heavy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So Mr. Zogaj, I want a clear answer. Between the two scenarios that I gave to you, that they were fleeing because of the attacks of the Serbian force or the actions, or they were fleeing because there was fighting between the KLA that was defending the village and the Serb forces, what was the reason that they left?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: At Bellanice on April the 1st, there was no KLA. There were no KLA positions. There never have been. I can say this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, you're not understanding the question. The question is that in your statement you said that several villages were attacked from 20 March on and that the villagers started to flee towards Belanica. I want to know what is the reason why the villagers started to go to Belanica. Was it because they were afraid, or they were leaving because of the attacks or because of the fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In the beginning, in March, a number of the civilian population left Suhareke. On the 25th of March, immediately after the NATO bombardment against Serbian targets in Kosova and Yugoslavia, the civilian population in Suhareke was in a miserable situation from the early hours of the morning onwards, and this continued for days on end. Other witnesses have testified to this as well. From this day, they came into Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Concentrate on the question that I'm making. What was the reason that the villagers left and they start going to Belanica? What were they afraid of? They were afraid of the attacks, or they were afraid about the fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The reason was because they found themselves being targets of continuous onslaughts, and that's why they came to seek shelter in our village. Whereas the KLA, which was protecting us, finding it impossible to defend its positions, withdrew tactically into other villages. And that is how the population at Bellanice came to find itself at the centre of Serbian police and army attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: My last question: You say that the reason was because they found themselves being targets -- being targets of continuous onslaught. Who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The civilian population? The civilian population was always the target of the police and the Serbian army. Beginning at 11.00 on the 1st of April, the situation was very desperate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You're free to go. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, can you please give the Court your full name. Excuse me. Do you want to put on your headphones?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: [In English] I do understand. [Interpretation] My name is Osman Kuci.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Kuci?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I was born in 1966, in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And Suva Reka is located in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: It is a municipality in its own. It belongs to the Prizren region.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you Albanian?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what's your profession?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I'm an interpreter from English into Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of May, and you gave a statement at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you were also interviewed on the 14th of June, 2001, and you gave a second statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: On the 3rd of February this year, you attended a meeting with members of the Office of the Prosecutor and an appointed officer of the Tribunal, and at that meeting you were provided with a copy of your statement, of the two statements, in the Albanian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to review and to confirm that the contents are true?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, just in order to correct a discrepancy between your two statements, can you please clarify to the Court: Which date did you leave Kosovo? Is it 27th of March or 27th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: 28th of March, a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I would like to submit the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 109.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. The summary of the witness's testimony is as follows: The witness worked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got a very brief issue for a clarification. Are the attachments a part of the statement which is tendered, or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The practice has been to admit those too, with the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I just wanted to be sure about that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So the summary of the witness's testimony is the following: The witness worked for the USKDOM and the OSCE-KVM mission in Suva Reka as an interpreter from November 1998 to March 1999. During this time, he saw a number of villages around Suva Reka that had been destroyed. Soon after the OSCE evacuated Suva Reka on 18 or 19 March 1999, the witness saw various military vehicles and materiel in the area. The witness lived close to the Balkan Hotel, which the Serb forces used as their headquarters. He observed the VJ wearing green camouflage uniforms and the MUP wearing blue camouflage uniforms. On the 27th and 28th March, 1999, the witness and many others were forced to leave their homes. The MUP told them to leave within five minutes or they would be killed. A convoy of cars and tractors was formed in Suva Reka, which headed in the direction of Albania via Prizren. En route, the witness saw houses burning. He also saw a number of Serb checkpoints and witnessed Serb police going up and down the convoy, robbing people. A uniformed policeman threatened to kill the witness unless he gave the police money. The witness also saw police stealing vehicles and forcing the people to continue on foot. He was told by Serb police to go to Albania. "That's your country." At the Albanian border, the witness had to hand over his documents and vehicle licence plates. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you graduate from university?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I have not attended university. I attended the higher pedagogical school at Prizren.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to use the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Milosevic. You're being asked to use the microphone. Is it on? If you speak --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's on. The light switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer. You said that you graduated from the higher pedagogical school in Prizren; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you spent your entire time living in Suva Reka, is that right, except for that short time you spent in Slovenia; otherwise you were living in Suva Reka? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes, in Slovenia and the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you and your brothers, between 1990 and 1998, opened a shop in Suva Reka, and that later on you opened a bar, a coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, linked to your business with respect to the shop and your catering establishment, the bar you worked in, was that in order? Did everything function normally?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No, not normally but in rather difficult situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why was it rather difficult? You say you had a shop. You had a bar afterwards. Now, what was difficult about the situation then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: There were difficulties coming as a result of the administration of the time, the taxes, financial police. All of them created difficulties for people in small businesses like myself and my brother. And we were unable to operate as the result of the administration of the time, which created a number of problems and obstacles for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I'm able to understand, you did work throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: We worked only to the extent that we could survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was the same for everybody, owners of shops or anybody who had any other business. But did you have a special problem perhaps that was not shared by everybody else in the country? When you -- or we talk about taxes and financial inspection and so on and so forth, did you encounter any specific problems?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes, mainly having to do with taxes and inspections from the financial police, which very often worked outside their remit. They wanted bribes, which we gave them. And police which were sheltered near our -- in a hotel near our shop, they often came and got commodities which they did not pay for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there shops and bars like that owned by Serbs or were they just own by Albanians, Albanian proprietors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: In that area, there were no shops where Serbs worked. There was only my shop and then that is what I can answer for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I was not interested in the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're not going to dwell on that then. When did you start working for the Kosovo diplomatic mission?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: As I've said in my statement, that was in 1998. October, November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But later on, you began working for the OSCE mission. What I'm asking you is how long you worked for the diplomatic mission before you became employed by the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: After two months, the diplomatic mission was transformed into the OSCE mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for those two months, you worked for the American Diplomatic Observer Mission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on, when it became integrated with the OSCE mission, did you continue working for the American part of that observer mission?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: When it was transformed into the OSCE, there was no American part. It was only known as the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the American observer mission, the one you worked for before working for the OSCE, were there you the only interpreter or were there other Albanians working as interpreters with the mission?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: At Suhareke, there were about 25 interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to draw the attention of the technical booth to the fact that I am getting interference between the two channels, the Albanian channel and the Serbian channel. So there seems to be a technical problem. This is something that I haven't had any trouble with so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see if that can be put right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to listen to the channels and see what I'm getting over channel 6, which is the Serbian interpretation. But let's continue. I assume that the technical booth will be able to put that right soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- were you doing the interpretation when members of the American observer mission had contacts with the representatives of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. No. I never had any meetings with the KLA in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on, while you were employed in the Verification Mission, did you do the interpreting for a meeting at which representatives of the Verification Mission talked to representatives of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to meet, in your capacity as an employee of KDOM or as an employee in the Kosovo Verification Mission, some representatives of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes. We saw members of the KLA on our patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the representatives of those missions, did they talk to them on that occasion or not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Sometimes they talked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the witness to draw near the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you translated for them; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci -- yes. You got the message.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. We also translated, when there was need, for members of the KLA or the Yugoslav army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How often did you interpret for the members of the KLA while you were working with the American KDOM?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, twice. And these were short meetings, meetings on the street, not official meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did those talks have to do with, at the brief meetings that you had which you say were not official meetings? What did they discuss?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I'm not competent to discuss the conversations that took place. I'm not an official who could explain what these conversations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you what was discussed, because those discussions went through you. So you physically had to hear both sides for you to be able to interpret.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Indeed. We interpreted for both sides. But we are not authorised to convey the substance of what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I have an explanation as to whether the witness is duty-bound to say what he knows here, or does he have the right to refrain? Because, as he has just said, in view of the fact that he took the solemn declaration here that he would speak the truth, what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Kuci, you're not authorised to say what was said in those conversations, what are you referring to? Was this something you signed when you joined the OSCE? Tell us what the authority is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the substance of the conversation, which is something I didn't take notes about, I think this is a matter for representatives of the OSCE. I haven't signed anything to say that I won't speak, but it's not my place to discuss the content of what was said between members of the KLA and the members of the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you told by anybody not to repeat the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was there a general rule in the OSCE that interpreters should not repeat conversations which they had to interpret? Was there any notion of confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally we had to maintain the confidentiality of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
