utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, can you assist us on this matter? As far as the OSCE is concerned, do you know of any policy or the like?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To be absolutely honest, Your Honour, I do not know of any policy, other than the one of general confidentiality, to which the witness has referred. It seems to me, however, that the witness is being brought forward to give evidence, and I know of no sort of Rule 70 basis whereby this evidence could not be elicited. If it does become a matter of a substance -- especially the context of what he's saying now - it wasn't an official meeting, it was on the street - I don't see how the Prosecution can take the view that we would be opposing. On the other hand, I cannot speak for the OSCE, other than this witness is under a general rule of confidentiality. But surely, when coming before this Tribunal to give evidence, unless it's covered by Rule 70, it's for Your Honours to decide as to whether or not he ought divulge the nature of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Ryneveld, if the evidence related to security matters, the OSCE itself would be interested in the confidentiality of that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And since I do not know what the subject matter of this conversation was any more than -- it's not in the statement. I'm not in a position to assist the Court on that matter other than I'm not aware of anything specific which prohibits this witness from testifying to those questions which the Court permits him to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, we'll hear what the evidence is. You are here, of course, to tell the truth, and we think that obligation overrides any general obligation. But if the question relates to security at all, or may relate to security of the OSCE, or something of that sort, then we will consider ordering the question not to be answered. We note that you say you took no notes of the conversation. If you can remember what was said, say so, but if you can't, say that you can't remember, if that's the position. But do your best to answer the questions, if they're relevant and you can answer them. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say that the OSCE had meetings and had published its report, became public. And the meetings where I was an interpreter were short encounters, for instance, on the street, where members of the OSCE met representatives of the KLA and asked what the situation was like: Is everything in order? Has there been any gunfire? And, for instance: Today Serbian police and army convoy passed in a certain direction. Or where the Yugoslav army was deployed. And from here, we would move on to other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So to summarise, these were short conversations, generally about the deployment of troops or forces, that sort of topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your assertion that these two conversations that you mentioned pertained exclusively, in terms of their substance, to the Serb side. Were there any conversations about, and did any of the subject matter pertain to that particular interlocutor's side, that is to say, the KLA? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Could you make the question clearer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that your explanation was that the contents of this conversation, that is to say, the questions and the answers between your employers and the representatives of the KLA, pertained exclusively to information related to the Serb side. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. There were also conversations with members of the KLA, between members of the KLA and the Yugoslav army, at checkpoints and the like, when a convoy of humanitarian aid had to pass, and the OSCE checked these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the conversations that you mentioned. What was the substance of that part of the conversations that related to the KLA, not the movement of convoys of the Serb army and police.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: The content of the conversation was, for instance: What's the situation like? Is there any gunfire? Are there any problems? These were the kinds of conversations we had, both with the KLA and with members of the Serbian forces. It was mainly members of the mission asking KLA members what the situation was like in their areas and where gunfire came from, if there was any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've been saying, can one infer that the members of the mission only put questions to the KLA that they encountered on the way that pertained to the Serb forces, or did they also ask questions that pertained to their forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: They asked members of the KLA if there had been gunfire, but they would also ask the Serbian forces if there had been gunfire. They would ask similar questions to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the people that you were interpreting for in KDOM? You met them. You worked with them for months. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I should say again that in KDOM and in the OSCE Verification Mission, there were lots of people, and I can't really remember their names. I'm not sure that I can discuss these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you worked with the same people during that time while you worked, or perhaps this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: We didn't work always with one person or with one team. We moved around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you work with the same team?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Normally, we worked for three days with the same team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three days. In three days you can probably establish who these people are. Can you say anything about who these people are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the relevance will be shown by my further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then ask your further questions to show the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these people civilians or military persons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: These people were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were civilians. Does that pertain both to KDOM and to the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes. All the people I met were civilians, and I didn't ask about their particular fields of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, in response to the question you asked me earlier, although I outlined our general position, I must say that the line of questioning now - and this is of course for the Court to determine - is completely outside the scope, other than passing reference to his employment, of the nature of the statement that this witness has been tendered for. In other words, I leave it to the Court to determine how relevant it is, but I want to note for the record that there is nothing in his statements about his work with the KDOM or OSCE. And I leave it to the Court, but I thought I should make that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've allowed the questions because the witness did work for them and there's been evidence about them. But so far, nothing very relevant has appeared. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Bear in mind you've got to show relevance for any of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No doubt the witness did mention in his statement that he worked for the American KDOM and then for the Kosovo Verification Mission. I think that the examinations of witnesses to date, notably of General Drewienkiewicz and Lieutenant Colonel Ciaglinski, indicated the relevance of the substance of the work of the Verification Mission, the presence of a large number of military personnel on the mission and also many elements that indicated that the mission largely focused on preparations for the NATO aggression. Since the witness worked for the mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is all a matter of argument, and you can make your submissions in due course. This witness said he worked for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that you met the members of the KLA only in the street. You would meet them only in the street. Where would you meet them? Can you determine that more specifically? What does "in the street" mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: On the street not in the sense of while walking around but in villages where groups of the KLA were, where they had checkpoints of various kinds, just as the police had in the areas controlled by the Yugoslav police and army. So that at the entrance to a village, there would be a checkpoint with two soldiers of the KLA. And this was the way in which we met people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you would enter a village, would you talk to any KLA members then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I didn't have any opportunity to talk to KLA commanders or members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you said that you were in these conversations twice, in these situations of conversations between your employers and representatives of the KLA, that that was at the time when you worked for the American KDOM. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. This was with the OSCE. When I was working for the American KDOM, I wasn't involved in conversations with members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. Let us continue with your statement. In paragraph 3, page 1, at the very end. Since you describe the number -- the colours of the uniforms of the army and the police, you say, "I was never in a position to see their shoulder patches. " Can I understand that to mean that you were not in any close contact with them since you used the word "never," that you could "never" see them? That is to say that you never had any close contact with the military or with the police, the kind of close contact which makes it possible for you to see their shoulder patches?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: You're referring to the Serbian army and police, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I am talking about your statement and what it contains; that is to say that you were never in that kind of contact with them that would make it possible for you to see their shoulder patches.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes. During work with the OSCE, yes, I was close. And the Serbian place had the blue camouflage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The examiner has moved on, and he's asking you about a passage in your statement, Mr. Kuci, when the OSCE had left and Serb forces moved in to Suva Reka and you were able to see various units in the town, and you said that the VJ wore green camouflage uniforms and the MUP had blue camouflage uniforms, but you said you were never in a position to see their shoulder patches. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is precisely what I want to clarify. During work for the OSCE, yes, we were was in close contact, and I was able to see the shoulder patches. But after the departure of the OSCE mission, it was only normal that I wasn't close enough, and I was only observing their positions at a distance, from my house. I could only see which one was a police uniform, which one was an army uniform, but I wasn't close enough to see that. I could only see that from the window of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, page 1 of the other statement, you say, and I'm going to quote the entire sentence: "I also wish to say that I was told that when the OSCE leaves Kosovo, I should hide so that the Serb police would not arrest me. It is for that reason that I never left my apartment." Who said to you that you should hide so that the Serb police would not arrest you? You say that you were told. Who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: The head of the OSCE mission in Suhareke said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you move on to say that you were aware that you might be killed. However, your statement shows that you were in contact with the police, that nobody arrested you, and that nobody harmed you. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: After the departure of the mission, it was obvious that an interpreter who should work for the OSCE could be a target. I personally was not harmed but perhaps others were killed. I know that I was threatened, as I've stated there in my statement. Just before passing the border, they put myself at gunpoint, and I could say that I was near death there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But your entire statement which refers to your departure and crossing the border refers to several contacts you had with the police, but nobody arrested you although they knew that you had worked for the OSCE. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I do not know how clear this is. When I left the house and until I reached the point, I'm not sure that every single policeman ought to have known that I worked for the OSCE. They might not. I was part of a convoy with other people that were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. It is quite clear that nothing happened to you. After all, that is something that you never claimed anyway. Towards the end of page 1, the third paragraph from the bottom - I'm referring to your second statement - you say that you travelled to Kukes with a person, a woman, who told you that the inhabitants of the village were told to go to Albania. That's what it says here. The police kept some of the men in the village. They were lined up at the school and executed. She did not see the execution. So that person did not see the execution that she told you about. So you heard about an execution from a person who is not an eyewitness of that execution herself. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: As stated there, she was there. She helped us. She wanted a lift in our tractor. As I said, she said that they held all the males and they let the women alone, as she has described it. The men were lined up for execution. So basically what I'm trying to say is that she left, she hasn't seen them, and I haven't seen them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to hear. Then towards the end of your statement, you say - your statement is short - the beginning of the second page: "The police and the army did not escort us except for the fact that we saw police cars on the way. Then we came to Prizren." And the last sentence in your statement reads: "We crossed without being insulted or ill-treated." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Actually, my family and myself were not ill-treated physically. On the route to Prizren, we saw Serbian police and civilian Serbs which were driving in the opposite direction at high speed. And as I've said, around Prizren we were insulted, with the specific words that I've mentioned there: "Go away. You'll never return. You asked for NATO to come in. NATO will help you now," and so on and so forth, and other words to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in the last sentence: "We passed without being insulted or ill-treated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is the border. Before that, he describes in the statement various incidents, including having to give them money. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. A few metres to the border where the convoy had been stopped -- because not everybody could pass speedily through. There was a very long convoy. So waiting in that convoy, there were two policemen who pointed their pistol towards me, and they asked me for my money or be killed, and I gave them money, as I've explained over there. The same happened to my brother. They threatened him with a pistol in his chest and took his money away. I consider this to be a grave insult. I do not know what kind of other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. insults you could be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting your own statement when I put these questions to you. As for what you have been claiming in terms of what happened to you, of course it would have been hard had it happened. However, during my cross-examination, I've been trying to establish what is true out of all the things that you've said. I can't find a particular section now, but didn't you write down here that you were a teacher for a time before you went into this other business?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: In Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which school did you work in Suva Reka? Elementary school, secondary school? Which school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Primary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The name of the school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: It was called the 7th of March, Shtate Mars school, in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many teachers were there in that school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, but it is about 50 or 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many pupils?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there 1.000 or 800 or 1.500 or ...

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Somewhere in the region of 800 to 1.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard enough now about education. It's no part of the witness's statement, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness said that he worked as a teacher, so since he worked as a teacher and since the question of education is greatly challenged in the case of some witnesses, I just wanted to ascertain that he worked in a school where there were about 850 pupils and about 50 or 60 teachers. So we're not going to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you make all your statements to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Which statements are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Statements of this kind, the ones that have to do with the events that you're testifying about for these purposes. Who did you give the statements to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: People who work for the Tribunal, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I have information that before giving a statement to the investigator working for this institution, that you gave a statement, on the 10th of April, 1999, to people from the International Crisis Group, and it is a statement of the 10th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I cannot remember having given any statement to the International Crisis Group. It could be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have made a note of this from the information that is accessible to me. In fact, you gave statements on three occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: The statements that I've given were mainly given to people working for this Tribunal. I cannot remember -- I'm not aware of ever having met members of the International Crisis Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness gave a statement to the -- he might not remember the institution. It was when he was in Tirana and it was for the ICJ. I have in hand two statements to the Croatians, and that was also disclosed to the accused and to the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you gave statements twice to representatives of the International Crisis Group, and in none of those statements did you make mention of the fact that the police stole cars in Zur. You mentioned that for the first time in the talk on the 16th of June, 2001. Why didn't you bring that matter up earlier on, these occurrences, if they did indeed take place?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: This did really happen. It could have been possible that when I gave the first statement, not everything came to my mind. In the second statement, I filled it up with more of what I was able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you can see in both these two statements, according to your own definitions that it didn't come to your mind, it didn't occur to you, it did not occur to you; it did not come to your mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's his answer: It didn't come to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since you worked for the Verification Mission and, before that, the KDOM - that is to say, without a doubt, you were one of the best-informed people around when it comes to the Albanian population in that area - now, do you know of an event that took place on the 21st of March, 1999, when, between 1800 hours, or rather, between 1440 hours and 1500 hours, and then later on, between 1800 and 1820 hours, Albanian terrorists opened fire on members of the police force who were in your municipality in the village of Rastani? Do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. On 21st of March, no doubt I was at home because the OSCE mission had left, as far as I remember, on the 12th of March. And after that time, I didn't go out on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did communicate with someone, I assume, and occurrences of that kind must have been something that was heard about because they were in the vicinity. So is your answer you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of this case because the village that you've mentioned is a long way from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know something else that took place in your municipality on that same day, in the village of Movljane, when cumulative missiles launched from a hand-held rocket launcher, members of the KLA once again hit a target and it was the police? Did you hear about that? On that same day. On that same 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. From my house, perhaps I heard gunfire in the area, but I know nothing about this specific case that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you mean when you say you might have heard? Did you hear or did you not hear about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I can say I did hear gunfire, but I don't know where they came from or who shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But, now, do you know about another event that took place in Suva Reka itself on the 22nd of March at 14.30 hours, in fact, in Suva Reka? The street's name was Cara Dusana. 46A, the number of the house. Albanian terrorists stormed the Balkanbelt shop - Balkanbelt Suva Reka is a well-known company - and shot Bogdan Lazic with several bullets. He was from the village of Sopina, but this took place in Suva Reka on the 22nd of March at 14.30 hours, which means right by you, where you were. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I said that after the 20th of March, I didn't leave my house until the date when I crossed the border to Albania. So I saw nothing of events of this kind and I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the killing of Elshan Sheqiri? He was born in 1937. And it took place in the village of Pecane in the municipality of Suva Reka. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. I didn't know this person, and I haven't heard of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear about the name of Kuci Namil [sic], also from Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again? I didn't hear the name properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The name is Kuci Namil [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what's question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is whether he has heard about him because he's from Suva Reka. And this man was killed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I -- this name Namil is not known to me. I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of the killing of a policeman by the name of Slobodan Petkov in the village of Pecane in your own municipality Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about these matters which he's putting to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've heard of none of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your evidence is you stayed in your apartment after the OSCE left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologise for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is very nearly up, but we'll let you ask another question if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to put something right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see the name properly. It wasn't Kuci Namil. It was Kuci Qamil. That was the name. There was a blur on my paper. Did you hear about him, Kuci Qamil from Suva Reka? His name was Kuci Qamil.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: I heard about this case after I returned from Albania. I didn't hear anything about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that from the beginning of 1998 onwards, up until the beginning of the war, that is to say the 24th of March and throughout the time that you were there, do you know that it was mostly Albanians who were killed by the KLA? And have you heard of the following name, Bajraktari Bafti from Budakovo, for example, who was killed in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. I have never heard of any of these names or incidents that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. No. You've had your extra question. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question, please. I have 20 names here, a list of 20 names of Albanians from the Suva Reka municipality who were killed by KLA terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, have you heard of a single Albanian who was killed by the KLA in the territory of your municipality? Do you want me to read out those 20 names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Can you answer the question? The question was: Have you heard of a single Albanian killed by the KLA in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't heard of any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the amici have no questions to ask Mr. Kuci. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just one matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, when you were describing the conversations that the KVM staff had with the KLA staff and the ones who were present, can you clarify if during the conversation there was any indication that the KVM was helping the KLA staff by saying where the VJ or the MUP positions were?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN KUCI
utterances.text: No. As far as I was present -- as far as my impressions went, the OSCE mission was unbiased and impartial and neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kuci, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, the Prosecution calls Hadije Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, Mr. Ryneveld, may I deal with some practical matters? Hearings this week. Tomorrow we'll be sitting from 9.30 to 4.00. On Friday, there will be a change to the programme which has been necessitated because of a change in circumstance. We will sit from 9.00 until sometime after 1.00, fairly shortly after 1.00. Just so that everybody should be warned of that. The other matter concerns the witness statements, and I'm not sure that we have yet got number 12 on the list of the 16th of April, Aferdita Hajrize. Now I may be wrong about that. Could you check it out? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We certainly well. Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. I believe that we have provided that particular statement yesterday to -- through the normal channels for the Court. I might also indicate, Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, that Exhibit 83, page 5 might be of some assistance to show the village where the next witness is from. Also on Exhibit 4, map 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Hadije Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And am I correct that you are presently an unmarried Muslim, ethnic Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what village did you reside in in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Turicevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you indicate for us, please, where your village is located? What's the nearest, closest town?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Skenderaj and Klina are roughly the same distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness please be shown Exhibit 83, at page -- page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, when the usher puts this map, you will see it on the screen in front of you, but I'm going to ask you to use the pointer --

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- and tell us if you can locate on the screen beside you, that is the map, where your village is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And it may assist the Court: If you look at page 5, the right-hand column, number 14, about two inches to the left of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you point that out for us, please?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, Witness. You're now pointing to a location where there seems to be a convergence of some roads and where it says "Turicevac"; correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Turicevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is in the municipality of what, Srbica?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. You can turn away. Thank you. Now, just a couple of other questions, if I may. I understand that you've lived there all your life. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what was your former occupation?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I worked at a book shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, did you give a statement to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 21st of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently, on the 4th of February of this year, 2002, were you provided with a copy of your statement in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at that time, did you appear before a presiding officer of the Court and tell that officer that the contents of your statement were true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement now be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour. I might, while we're awaiting distribution, indicate that I have provided a copy of a skeleton summary of that for the benefit of the translators, and I believe the Court may also have a copy. If I may, I propose to read that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get an exhibit number first, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, this witness in her statement describes that her village has roughly a hundred houses and a total population of about a thousand people. She describes that it's about 12 kilometres from the town of Srbica and about 13 kilometres from Klina. It indicates that the KLA had headquarters in the village, at the school, and when NATO bombing began, many refugees from Prekaz had already sought refuge in Turicevac. She goes on to describe that on the 26th of March, 1999, at roughly 9.00, Serb forces began shelling Turicevac from the direction of Broje. Villagers and refugees, including the witness, fled in a convoy heading toward Tusilje, also in the Srbica municipality, where many other refugees had sought refuge. Well, apparently, Serb forces eventually surrounded Tusilje on the 29th of March, 1999, at roughly 8.00 a.m. They approached from both Klina and from Srbica. The police arrived first, on foot, firing their weapons, followed by the army in tanks and other vehicles. At 10.00, the police and military began directing the refugees through towards Klina. En route through to Tusilje, more than 1.500 men were separated from their families and sent to Srbica, where Serb forces questioned them in the local school. The women, children, and elderly continued toward Klina, passing soldiers with tanks and armoured vehicles. En route to Klina, the witness and her family left the convoy for their own village. Although the village had been burned and damaged, they stayed at their family home for two days. Many other refugees came to the village, and on the 1st of April, 1999, the police arrived in civilian cars that they had stolen from Kosovo Albanians. They killed three people in the village, sent the remainder toward Klina in a convoy of more than a thousand. Along the route, the witness saw burned villages and bodies of men and older boys. After stopping in other villages overnight and along the way, on the 2nd of April, 1999, the witness and her group arrived at Klina. Police in Klina directed them onto trucks driven by gypsies, heading towards the village of Volujak. Tanks and troops lined the road to Volujak, and from there they walked towards Djakovica. The police didn't stop the refugees, but maintained checkpoints along the road. When the convoy arrived at Djakovica, walking through the city's outskirts, the witness saw neighbourhoods on fire, shops damaged and destroyed. The witness and her group followed the other refugees from Djakovica, suspecting they would know the quickest route to the border. They were not provided with food or water, and the witness heard that young women taken from the convoy had probably been raped and ill-treated. On the 4th of April, 1999, the refugees left Djakovica and walked to the border crossing of Qafe e Prushit. There she saw a large presence of Serb forces on the road from Djakovica to the border, and the Serb forces told the refugees that the area on either side of the road was mined and that they should hurry to the border, as NATO might attack. To reach the border, the refugees had to climb a steep hill, leaving some of the elderly and sick behind. That is the general outline of her statement, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now. Cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I also, at the beginning of the next session, raise a brief issue with the Court about clarification of the Court's interpretation of the number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By all means. Ms. Fazliu, we're going to adjourn now for an hour and a half. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence in the adjournment and until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecuting team. Would you be back, please, at half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a ruling of the Trial Chamber on the facilities provided for the accused for his defence. The procedural background is as follows: The accused has, on a number of occasions, complained about the lack of facilities available to him to conduct his defence. Further to an undertaking given by the amicus curiae on the 27th of February, the amici curiae filed a "Brief on the provision of adequate facilities to allow the accused to prepare his defence," and on the 6th of March, 2002, the Trial Chamber ordered the Registry to provide a report on the facilities available to him. This report was filed on the 18th of March and was discussed during public session on the 10th of April, at which time both the accused and the amici curiae made various observations as to the adequacy of the facilities provided. Article 21 of the Statute sets out certain minimum guarantees to which an accused appearing before the Tribunal is entitled, including the right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the report from the Registry relating to the facilities provided to the accused and is satisfied that all possible efforts are being made to assist him. As a general principle, the accused is treated in the same way as all other accused. Any variations have been put in place by the Registry in an attempt to assist him in light of the fact that he wishes to conduct his own defence. First, and contrary to the repeated assertions of the accused, he is not and never has been kept in isolation. He is allowed to mix with other detainees at the Detention Unit and to receive visits in accordance with the standard procedures. As a result, the accused receives regular visits from members of his family and from representatives of various organisations. The regime for legal visits - by which I mean visits that are fully confidential - has been complicated by the fact that, for many months, the accused refused to identify those persons with whom he wished to communicate and then, when such visits were offered by lawyers that he had asked to meet, he declined to communicate with those persons. That position is now resolved following the appointment of two persons as his associates, and the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused has adequate facilities for the preparation of his defence, as guaranteed by Article 21 of the Statute. The accused can now meet with his two associates on a confidential basis at the Tribunal during breaks in the court proceedings and at the Detention Unit at the end of the day. The length of these visits is governed by the regulations in place at both the Detention Unit and the Dutch prison in which it is located, which apply to all detainees and their counsel. He can also communicate freely with the two associates by telephone from the Detention Unit, including at the weekend; and, as an exception not available to other detainees who have appointed Defence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. counsel, by telephone from the Tribunal during the day. The associates can help the accused in making photocopies and sending faxes at the premises of the Tribunal during the day and limited facilities are also available to do this at the Detention Unit. In addition to facilities similar to those provided to the other detainees, the Registry also provides additional copies of documents served in the proceedings for him to discuss with his associates. The accused may review video material and use a computer in his cell, although for security reasons it is not permitted for any accused to have e-mail and Internet access. Yes. That concludes the ruling. Mr. Ryneveld, there was a matter you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Actually two matters, if I may. The first is a response to Your Honour's question to me this morning about the witness statement. Our records indicate that we in fact had produced the witness statements of that witness to the Senior Legal Officer on the 19th of April and then additional copies were provided on the 22nd of April. So hopefully copies of that witness statement have made their way to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That appears to be the position, I now understand, but equally, we've made no ruling upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we will, at an appropriate time, have to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand that. I was just responding to your issue about getting the statement to you for review so you could make a ruling. Thank you. The second matter, Your Honour, deals with a comment by the Court, I believe it was last Monday, concerning the 90 witnesses. And just so that I'm completely clear about to what extent the Court is referring to 90 witnesses, my understanding was, back on the 11th of January and the 9th of January, when the issue of witnesses came up -- I've checked the record, and the Court asked me to deal with a point in the order, and I indicated to the Court that we then anticipated calling 110 witnesses by way of viva voce evidence, of the potential 201 that we had put in our 65 ter filing. I then outlined to the Court the numbers and how they were broken down.
