Then, at that time, the Court clarified with me how I arrived at the 110 figure, and the exchange went something like this: "JUDGE MAY: In the document, there are numbers for the live witnesses, and there appear at the moment to be 90 live witnesses that you've numbered, with the possibility of a further 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would that be right? That's your 110?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's my 110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then we have your 92 bis, your written statements, and they number up to - is this right - to 123?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct." The Court then indicated: "JUDGE MAY: We consider that a total of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm apologising to the interpreters for reading too fast. "JUDGE MAY: We consider that a total of 90 witnesses should be sufficient, having regard to size and complexity of the case, but that will not prevent you from making the application during the trial for additional witnesses, on good cause, for challenge, if the witnesses come forward." And then the Court went on to talk about looking at the 92 bis statements. In the written order of the 11th of January, the Trial Chamber set out: "The Trial Chamber sets the number of witnesses the Prosecution may call in person at 90, with leave to apply to the Chamber for permission to present additional witnesses. 2. The Trial Chamber --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Would you mind reading out a bit more slowly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I've again been cautioned to read more slowly. "Secondly, the Trial Chamber instructs the Prosecution to review the proposed list of witnesses whose evidence is to be presented by way of statements pursuant to 92 bis so as to avoid repetition, and orders that the applications for admission of such evidence be made forthwith on completion of the certification and translation processes." Now, I've read that by way of background, Your Honour, just to see -- because it makes a lot of difference to our planning whether we are in fact restricted to a total of 90 witnesses. My understanding was that we were restricted to a total of 90 live witnesses, plus consideration to be given for 92 bis. Now, we've cut down that 90 live witnesses considerably, and we've also cut down our anticipated 123 92 bis witnesses considerably, but the total of both of them will exceed 90 witnesses. That's the problem. And we were thinking that the question now becomes whether what was a 92 bis witness, because of the procedure we're now adopting, is interpreted by the Chamber to have become a live witness. That's my problem. I assumed not, and I've been operating on the basis that the 92 bis witness is not included in the total. Now, it may be somewhat academic, in light of the fact that we have a finite date whereby we have to complete all our witnesses. I understand that. But I just hope that I'm not at cross-purposes with your order to think I'm allowed up to 90 live witnesses plus 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I think that the circumstances are different from those in which we originally made the order. First of all, when we made the order, it related to Kosovo alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The second matter is that the procedure which has now been adopted relating to 92 bis witnesses, which was not one foreseen at the time, it would seem to me sensible to review the whole matter again, in the light of the present circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would certainly appreciate that. It's just that when Your Honour mentioned the other day that I was restricted to 90, I had to ask for clarification. So if Your Honours are prepared to reconsider, in light of the developments that have happened, and give us further guidance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- keeping in mind you have indicated July 19 is the target date for completion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- I'd be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could assist us by making an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- for review of the order and we can then review it in light of the all the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll do that as soon as we possibly can. Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to what you've said, I just want to clarify the facts of the matter. Actually, I didn't ask for anything. I just wanted it to be made quite clear that I have been prevented from having what I call normal means of ensuring an equality, the way it is understood anywhere in the world, and everything that you have been insisting upon allegedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not prepared to enter into further discussion about it. That was a ruling. We will look into the matter of the telephone. Now, if there's some fresh matter you want to raise, you can, but we're not going to go back over what we've dealt with already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I won't deal with the obvious. But I want to draw your attention to a few facts, a few material facts that are not in line with what you have received reports on and what you've just read. The question of isolation, you said a few minutes ago loud and clear in public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not prepared for continued submissions on this point. You raised an issue today about the telephone. We will have that looked into further, although we understand that you've been phoning unauthorised numbers and that's why you haven't got through. But we will check that out. Now, that that I read out was a ruling. We've considered all the matters, and there's no point going on arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not speaking about your ruling at all. Your ruling is your own affair. I just want to explain that the facts stand differently. Namely, you said that is what they wrote out for you, that I was never in isolation. I was in isolation for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We -- we are not prepared to enter into further argument about this. We've had the matter looked into, and we've given this ruling and that, for the moment, is that. If you want to make an application, another application, in due course, we'll consider it, but there's no point arguing about it today. We're going to go on with the evidence. If you have some further application about the telephone, you can make it tomorrow morning if it's not working and you're ringing the authorised numbers. There's no point continuing debate. We will have the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Do you know that I am the only detainee who receives even family visits in the presence of prison officials? Are you aware of that at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have looked into the various complaints you've made, and you've heard the answer. Now, that is an end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is here. We're going on with -- we're going on with the evidence. Now, would you like to take a seat. Now, do you want to ask this witness any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that your village is a small village numbering about 100 houses and that in it, during the war, 1999, there was the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in the school building of your village was the KLA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you know, does it mean that this led to a conflict between the army and police and the KLA that was in your village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: About what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the village there was a KLA unit, and in the school, according to your own assertion, was the KLA headquarters. So that is where the KLA was. And there was a conflict with the army and the police, between the KLA and the army and police.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: There was no conflict between the KLA and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the village, according to your own assertion, was a KLA unit with its headquarters in the primary school.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: There was a KLA presence. But when we were expelled, there was -- there were no clashes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that the Serb forces, on the 26th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. March -- that on the 26th of March, you left your village because the Serb forces shelled it. Were they shelling the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: They were shelling the houses, the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were they shooting at the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What she says is they were shelling the houses. That's what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But further on, in the next sentence, you say: "I do not remember that someone was hurt." Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Are we referring to the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is in this same paragraph, the sixth paragraph from the top. It says: "On the 26th of March, I left my village because the Serb forces shelled it." The next sentence goes on: "I do not remember that someone was hurt or wounded."

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do while you lived in the village before the war started? What were you doing? What are you, professionally speaking, by vocation?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I finished the high school of commerce, and I worked as a saleswoman at a book shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked with books, newspapers. You listened to the radio and television. I assume that you were informed about things that were going on. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, in view of your job and the education that you have, I assume that you were well-informed about events in your municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Depends what kind of situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean regular life, things that go on, everything that goes on. You're an educated person. You work at a book shop. You communicate with people. So I assume that you are a well-informed person. Is my assumption right or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After leaving your village on the 26th of March, you returned on the 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what is written in your statement, you did not see who killed people in the village of Josanica and how.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: People at Jashanice? Yes. I have seen dead people. It's all but natural that the police killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you did not see whether they were killed by the police or whoever. You simply did not see who killed them and how.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I have seen dead people. It's only to be assumed on who killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any bombing in your neighbourhood, in that area? I mean bombing coming from the air.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of what you were able to see and hear for yourself with your very own ears in view of all the noise and shooting and everything, were there any conflicts, any clashes between the KLA and the army and police?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Even before that, we came under shelling. So this was not the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before what?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Before the 26th. Ever since the case of Likoshan, we had been expecting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in Likosane?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I wasn't at Likoshan, but other members of my family who were at the burial were there. I wasn't there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even before the clash took place, that is to say the clash between the army and police and the KLA, your village was shelled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. I didn't say it had been shelled before this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I thought you said that that's what happened even before, a moment ago. Did the KLA withdraw from the village together with you or did they take a different direction?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: What date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The day you left the village, the 26th of March. That was the first time you left the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first question -- the first question is did the KLA leave the village on the 26th of March? Or perhaps even before that, were the KLA in the village on the 26th of March or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them on that day of the 26th of March when I left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the road from Djakovica to the border, according to what you say, nothing happened to you.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers told you that there was the danger of NATO bombing the area and that you should hurry up and take shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: If we had stayed in our own homes, there wouldn't have been any need to find shelter somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the time you were at the border, because that is the event that you testify about in your statement.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: But they expelled us by force. We didn't go of our own free will. We didn't even know the road to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you don't explain the fact that anybody forced you. Did anybody escort you? Did anybody force you to move towards the border? Was anybody with you, either towards the border or across the border?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: But of course we were forced, because nobody leaves their own house normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there was shooting in your village. You said that yourself. You said there was shooting in your village.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I didn't say there was an exchange of fire. There was shooting from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you claim that the KLA, who you say was in the village and had a headquarters in the village, did not shoot at the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: They didn't have equipment, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation of that. I apologise. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What she said was: "They didn't have the equipment, no doubt."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that the KLA wasn't armed? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: They had light weapons, yes, but in comparison with the Serbs, they had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May we take it, then, that what you're saying is that they didn't do any shooting, that they didn't shoot at the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I heard a lot of things, but I was unable to distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the events that took place in 1998 and 1999? For example, in January 1998, in your village, an attack was launched on Jordan Nicic, a forester, and it was a state-owned company called Serbia Sume. Do you know about that? It was by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: There's no forest in my village, and I don't know about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know about that case, let me ask you: Is your village the village of Turicevac?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 27th of January, 1998, it was precisely in the village of Turicevac, that is to say, in your own village, that there was an attack on Veroslav Vukojcic, from Raska, who had come there with his truck at 11.30 on the 27th of January, 1998? The village of Turicevac. That's where it happened.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: It didn't happen in Turicevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that on the 12th of February, at 10.00, in the village of Turicevac, a Bulgarian citizen by the name of Angel Borisov was attacked? At the time, they were arrested by the KLA but were released later. Do you know about that event? The 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard of it. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Murat Dajkaj, that name? Is it familiar? From the village of Rakitnica?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the attack, as you have not heard of that man who died in the attack, but the attack was on the 20th of February, in the village of Lausa, which is in the same municipality as your own village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard about another attack that also took place on the 20th of February, 1998, in Lausa, when Milorad Ristic was killed, from Djakovica? Other people were wounded. I don't want to mention their names. But he was killed. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the following name: a man called Taci Rizi, who was seriously wounded on the 5th of March, 1998? Have you heard about him? Do you know him? Also wounded by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't know of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you happen to hear of an incident that was linked to the attack on a diplomatic vehicle belonging to the Japanese embassy, where Ataka Gashabi [phoen], attache of the embassy in Yugoslavia, was in the car? She was not hurt. But this was on the 27th of April, in Lausa, in 1998. Do you remember that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: We are a long way from Lausa, and I don't know what cases may have happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you never heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it would seem fairly pointless to go on asking questions about this. The witness has said that she doesn't know what happened in Lausa. You asked her about ten incidents or so and she doesn't know about them. As I've said often before, you can put your evidence in front of us in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Just a few more questions to wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a single case of a crime perpetrated by members of the KLA in your village or in your municipality, that is to say, the Srbica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then there's no sense in asking you any more questions, any more specific questions in that regard, because you say you know nothing about it all. Just one more question, then. You said that at the border, they didn't ask you for any identity papers or any money. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and be brief. I just have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Fazliu, I have your statement here in my hands, and on page 2, paragraph 4 of that statement -- you have already commented on the matter in answer to a question from Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, but you do say in one particular spot that people kept joining the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you about what happened in your village. Can you tell us, please, roughly, how many KLA members were there in your village? A rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't know. I never was in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4, Your Honours, paragraph 3, you say in your statement, as recorded in it, that: "We were afraid that they might send us to a factory and that that factory might be bombed." So you were afraid that some of you might be bombed under certain circumstances, bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: We weren't scared of NATO; we were scared of the rapes that we heard took place at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but you said in your statement - and I don't know where you got that information from. Could you explain that to us, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please? - that you were afraid they wouldn't [as interpreted] send you to a factory that might be bombed. Now, did you hear of any factories having been bombed and people losing their lives? I don't know where you got that information from, that that was what you were afraid of. "We were afraid that they would send us to a factory," et cetera. That's the part.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said that they sent -- I said that they sent the population among factories and anything might happen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, you said that you had a small radio and that you listened to the news. Was it over that radio that you had heard about things like that happening, that is to say, that factories were being bombed and people killed?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's another point I want to ask you about linked to that fear, and it is on page 5, paragraph 3, and I would conclude with that. It is on that page of your statement, the statement you gave. You said that when you were at the border itself, that you noticed that the army was afraid of the NATO bombing. Is that something -- the conclusion you arrived at on your own or what grounds did you have for saying that, rather?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: But of course they were afraid. We had no reason to be afraid of NATO because we asked for NATO ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But if they bombed the soldiers there, the military there, some of you could have got killed too. Was that the reason you were hurrying, because of this fear?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I wasn't scared of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go, Ms. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I propose to call Sadik Januzi as our next witness. And while this witness is coming, might I invite Your Honours and the accused and the amici to turn to page 5. Rather than show this on the ELMO for the witness, I don't propose to deal anything -- he has difficulty reading. So page 5 of Exhibit 83. His village, as you will hear in due course, is Broje, and you will find that just to the left of the village, of previous village of Terasovac, just a quarter of an inch or half an inch to the left, at number 14, which is a marginal numbering on page 5. I also propose, if I may, to read the solemn declaration for him in English and have it translated over his earphones, if that meets with the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you just stand up for the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel is going to read something out to you. It will be translated, and would you say it after the interpreter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I will declare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Witness, just repeat after me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, would you state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Name and surname, Sadik Tahir Januzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And Mr. Januzi, is it right that you are a -- a Muslim ethnic Albanian, born in Broje in 1933?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And is Broje in the municipality of Skenderaj?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How many children do you have, sir?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I have six daughters and one son, married.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I understand that you are now a retired farmer and that you were formerly a security guard?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Now, sir, do I understand correctly that you were visited by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 23rd of April, 1999, at which time you gave a statement? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on the 21st of October of 2001, did they come to you and ask you to provide a second statement about -- a follow-up statement about what you told them earlier?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then, sir, just a few months ago, on the 2nd of February of this year, did you appear before a presiding officer of this court, and did you have available two copies of an Albanian translation of those statements and have them read out to you?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, did you sign -- or did you agree that the statement was true to the best of your recollection and belief?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: It was correct, exactly what I'd said, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might those two statements or the 92 bis statement now be tendered as exhibit -- I think we're up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 111. Thank you. While that's being done, might I read out a skeleton trial summary or do you wish me to wait? Your Honour, the statements that are being distributed are in two parts. In his first statement, this witness describes the situation in Broje in March of 1998 when the police set up checkpoints. Then following an incident when a policeman was killed by the KLA, the Serb forces started shelling his village. He describes an ongoing offensive by Serb forces during which time they attacked about 52 villages in the Drenica region and repeatedly shelled his village of Broje. As a result, the witness and his family were forced to constantly move from village to village over a period of 14 months. He describes in March 1999 Serb forces were shelling Broje and other surrounding villages. And then around the 24th of March, 1999, he and his family sought shelter in Izbica. Four to 5.000 residents from other villages also gathered in Izbica, and they could see the nearby village of Lecina burning. On the 27th of March, he saw Serbian soldiers setting fire to houses in Izbica. The following day, the 28th of March, at about 1.00 in the afternoon, Serbian forces surrounded them, gathered 5.000 people in a meadow which was about 150 metres from the village itself. He tells of soldiers demanding money under threat of burning their homes. He describes the men being separated from the women and children. An officer in charge told the soldiers to not let any of the men leave. The men were divided into two groups of about 70 each. One group went to a stream and the other was taken up the hill. The witness's group was ordered to go up the hill in two rows, escorted by ten soldiers. The soldiers were hurrying them with their machine-guns. The men in his group ranged between 40 and 96 years of age. At one point, a soldier told them to stop and ordered them to turn around, and he then heard one of them say, "Fire." Then the men started falling down, all shot from behind. He says it lasted a few seconds. The witness fell down, although he was not hit, and three dead bodies fell on his back. He could hear the soldiers checking whether anyone was still alive and then recounts hearing seven or eight additional pistol shots fired by the soldiers. Then he heard one of them saying, "Let's go. Our work is over." He describes crawling away and hiding in fear when he was joined by some other survivors, following which he went to his sister's house in Klladernica where he stayed for three or four days. On the last night of his stay at Klladernica, Serb forces started shelling that village before sunrise. All the young men fled to the forest, and he learned that the women from surrounding villages had found shelter in the school building in Klladernica, so he went to check on them. Shelling was still going on, and he saw three wounded people. And around 10.00, the Serb forces surrounded the school building and ordered the women, children, and elderly to proceed to Albania. In his second statement, which I will be very brief about, he describes in considerable detail leaving Klladernica on foot towards Klina and Gjakove and on to Prizren, without any food, in a convoy consisting of about 10.000 to 12.000 villagers, escorted by Serb forces. After describing in further detail what happened along the route, they eventually arrived at a village not far from Prizren. The Serbian policemen then said they would be taken by bus to the border. After an hour, a bus came and took them to the border at Zur on the 15th of April, 1999, where money was demanded from them and their personal documents were taken away. That is a very brief summary of his two statements, and I have no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Januzi, when the police established a checkpoint in your village, you did not leave the village then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: We left that day they came. We stayed until the evening, just before dusk, and then we went, came back, and then we returned home to eat supper. Before morning, before it was dawn, we went out again, and we put our lives at risk. Up on the furthest hill, at that stage, Nibarici's [phoen] family was buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Januzi, could you just deal with the questions you're asked, please, because we can get on more quickly that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Okay. I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about March 1998, that is to say, the appearance of the police in Brocina [phoen], or rather, the establishment of the checkpoint in March 1998. That did not disturb your everyday farm work; is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: It disturbed us, because there was sporadic gunfire in the early hours of the morning and in the evening, so we had to leave our houses early, at dawn, and return in the evening to eat and to have a little rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which date are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: From the moment they were stationed there on the 5th of March, 1998. That's what I mean. From that moment onwards, there was absolutely no improvement in the quality of life in my village. The whole family had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you continued with your usual farm work. On page 2 of your statement, in paragraph 2, it says that. It doesn't mention gunfire, only the establishment of a checkpoint, which did not disturb you in your regular life. That's the way it is according to your own statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, Your Honour, if the accused is referring to the second paragraph, since the accused does not have a statement, can't read it, I think that the sentence about "used to shoot sporadically in the air" ought to be put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continued working when the checkpoint was withdrawn to another village, and that is when we thought that we were a bit safer and started working. But when there was gunfire from there as well - heavy artillery was used, mortars and so on - it was more difficult in Broje, and that is why, on the 25th of March, we left and started getting together about 7.000 to 8.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 25th of March which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about 1998, several times, because the checkpoint was established in March 1998, that is to say, a year earlier. As for this year, judging by your statement, you did not have any problems then.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That year, 1998, we had problems. There was sporadic gunfire in that region. People were being buried. One man and two women were buried in the village of Vojnik. The family of Avni Bajriqi is another case. And that same year of 1998, there was no security at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I will phrase my question very carefully. You did not leave the village before a Serb policeman was killed in that village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: The policeman was brought in the hills of the village of Resnik. I do not know who killed him. I only know that from the date I'm referring to, there's no peace in this household, so we had to spend our life in the woods, coming back home before dusk and then leaving the house again before dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your village, at that time there was the KLA. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: There was a KLA, but not in my village. There's no wooded areas in my village, i.e., no basis for a war. It is in the open. For it to have a basis, we need to have wooded areas to hide in there. But neither the people nor the KLA would have been in a position to be there, because the terrain is inappropriate for war. There was a KLA present, but not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that they took away a policeman into the hills but that you did not know who killed him. If there was no KLA in the village, who was it that took the policeman into the hills?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I haven't followed this incident. I didn't follow what the KLA was doing. I was dealing with my family. My family has ten members, and I was concerned with gathering them together, and then in Klladernica, and then we went off to Albania. These were my concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a short while ago you said that a policeman was taken into the hills. That's what you said, not me. And since you say, "They took a policeman into the hills," my question is: Who took a policeman into the hills?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am just asking: What is the noun that stands next to the verb "did"? Or when it says, "They took him." So what's the noun preceding "took"? What's the subject? Who is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't help you further. He says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know that the policeman was killed by the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, several times you left Brocina and went back to Brocina, together with your family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right. That went on for almost a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise we heard, a few minutes ago, from your summary, that you went through different villages in that area during that year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in those different villages, then, did you encounter many members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I was a refugee and I had left my own village. I had become a refugee, among friends. I didn't see the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that throughout your area, that is to say this area around Srbica, there were a lot of KLA members? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Skenderaj is 13 kilometres away from me. Thirteen kilometres. That's along the paved road, apart from another kilometre and a half to my own house. I don't know what happened in Skenderaj. I didn't go there any time during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about Srbica. I said in the Srbica area, in the municipality where you were. I did not ask you about the town of Srbica itself, because I heard from this summary that we heard at the outset that you passed through 52 villages, if I heard it correctly. Fifty-two villages in your area. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I stayed about seven or eight months in Klladernica and then I stayed in Turjan, where I had friends. There we felt safer because of the forest nearby. It was better wooded than my village. I didn't stay a single day in Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you lived in the municipality of Srbica. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: That's right. We lived in that municipality, but on the border with the municipality of Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "Srbica," I'm referring to the municipality of Srbica and not the town of Srbica. We heard from the Prosecution that you passed through 52 villages during that year or year and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It must be a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may correct it since I authored the summary and not the witness. The forces attacked 52 villages. As a result of that, the witness moved from village to village. I didn't suggest that he moved to all 52 villages. It's my summary and not the witness's statement. What's correct is what's in his statement, and the accused has that at paragraph 2 and 3. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] All right. Then I misunderstood this, that the Prosecutor was speaking of the witness's testimony, because he did invoke the witness's statement when he referred to 52 villages. So he spoke of something that the witness did not refer to in his own statement. This created that confusion on my part. Let us proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I did not confuse. What I said in the summary is: "He describes an ongoing offensive by Serb forces during which time they attacked about 52 villages in the Drenica region and repeatedly shelled his village of Broje." Next sentence: "As a result, the witness and his family were forced to constantly move from village to village over a period of 14 months." That is what I said. The accused has made a connection somehow that the witness travelled through 52 villages. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. It's the statement which is the evidence. Nothing that the Prosecutor says is evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just explain. If I made a mistake, I made it because I assumed that the summary is a summary of the witness's statement, not of anything else. So could you please explain this to me? Is the summary a summary of the witness's statement or does it contain any other kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been explained to you often enough before. Now, do you want to ask the witness any more questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the killing of Blagoje Jovanovic in the village of Kostrc in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: It's not near my village. There was my village and then there was Turicevc, Kopilic i Eperm, and then Klladernica and then Kostrc. I don't know about this. I only --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know when the members of the KLA - that was on the 13th of June, 1998 - set on fire 12 Serb houses of the family of Smigic in the village of Leocina, and when they abducted five members of the Smigic family? Have you heard of this case? Are you aware of that? This was in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I don't know of this case, because I was with a great crowd of seven or eight members of the family, old people, women, children. We all gathered together, thinking -- we thought that nobody would do anything to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about when the members of the KLA attacked the village of Rudnik, when they set houses on fire, the houses of Radivoj Kovacevic and Nicifor Kovacevic on the 15th of June 1998? Do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this. I have no knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge concerning the killing of Zivojin Milic from the village of Sibovac? And actually, he was killed by the village of Trnavci on the 17th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of this. I don't know anything about this matter at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Milosevic, it seems a fairly pointless exercise to go on asking questions when the witness knows nothing about it, as he's made plain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously witnesses hardly know a thing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But then if you don't know anything about this, if you do not remember, have you at least heard of the attack on the 26th of March, 1999, in the village of Likovac when policemen were killed, namely Milan Pavlovic, Dusan Trifunovic, Ljubivoje Zivkovic, Dragivoje Gajic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point -- there's no point reading out these names. Do you know anything, Mr. Januzi, about this matter that's being put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have no knowledge of these things, of the things asked because I was only trying to look after my own family. I only saw Klladernica, as I said a little before. That's where I had my sister, friends. And then in that smaller village of Turjan and Klladernica. I don't know anything about Likofci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about any crime, any killing, any torching of houses, any abduction, any similar crime that was carried out by members of the KLA in your area, either against the Serbs or against the Albanians? Are you aware of any such crime?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of these things. I don't know. I only know what I have declared is correct. It is true, and I don't deny anything that I have stated. As for other villages, who was killed, I don't know. Nor have I put anything like that in my statement, nothing about the village of Likofci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think there is no point in putting any further questions to this witness, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have the amici got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall truly try to be brief for the same reasons. Let me just dwell on two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sadik, when you spoke of something that we already dealt with, this offensive that had been launched against 52 villages, as a matter of fact, was all of this in Drenica?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you explain what "offensive" means? Were these clashes between the KLA and the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about clashes of this kind. I know that there was slaughter and that I fled with my family. And I was just trying to preserve my family. And I don't know about these things. And what happened in the war, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All of this was in 1998? All the things that you spoke of here, the offensive, all of that was in 1998? And this led to --

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this led to you going from village to village for 14 months. It was because of that offensive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more thing. This second statement of yours, the 21st of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your benefit, this is the second statement, page 3, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Over here you talked about the 12th of April, when you set out, when you wanted to leave the place where you were, and then you came to the neighbourhood of Djakovica. And now you stated -- you stated the following --

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Can you please not try and get away from what I've spoken about? On March the 28th, 1998, I'm the only survivor of what happen at Izbica, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and you are veering away into other statement. Please, what I've stated over there, let's focus on those, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We've got your statement, and it's been summarised and we've read it. So you need have no fear that the Court hasn't got it and hasn't read it. But counsel just wants to ask you something shortly about a second statement which you made, and perhaps you'd just listen to him, and if you can, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I would like to do, sir. Indeed I do not wish to confuse you. You said at a particular point in this statement that a soldier who was there at that place where you were said to you that you should not wait there because NATO would bomb the bridge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes. What I have written there is true and correct. They told us, "Go away from here, because NATO could bomb." However, it would have been best for us to have been allowed to get through there and reach the Qafe e Prushit rather than having to travel for about 80 kilometres without no food or anything at all, through Gjakove, through Prizren, 35 kilometres, 80 kilometres, or whatever the distance is. It would have been better to have been allowed to get through the Qafe e Prushit. And they wouldn't allow us. They turned us back. It was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sadik, I just want to ask you one more thing. Again in the same place, you said, "When we moved three kilometres away, I saw a NATO aeroplane and I heard the sound of it. I saw the smoke when the bridge was bombed." Is that correct? I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Three -- about five or six kilometres from where we were. Yes, that was true. I'm not changing anything of what I've written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So did this make you seek shelter, move away from there fast?

utterances.speaker: SADIK JANUZI
utterances.text: Not very fast. We didn't leave speedily because the family had to go and try and get some food. It had gone three days without any food. So they weren't running or delaying. That was about 10 or 15 minutes, that interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't asked about what I went through at the Izbica massacre, it would appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Januzi, we have in fact -- as I said, we've got your statement before us. We've seen what you went through. We've heard it summarised. We've been able to read about it. And that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Tomorrow morning, half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of April 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 25
